'''Robert Adrain''' (30 September 1775 – 10 August 1843) was an Irish political exile who won renown as a mathematician in the United States. He left Ireland after leading [[Society of United Irishmen|republican]] insurgents in the [[Irish Rebellion of 1798|Rebellion of 1798]], and settled in [[New Jersey]] and [[Pennsylvania]]. With [[Nathaniel Bowditch]], he shares the distinction of being the first scholar to publish original mathematical research in America. This included his formulation of the [[method of least squares]] while working on a [[surveying]] problem (in two proofs of the exponential law of error published independently of [[Carl Friedrich Gauss]]) for which he is chiefly remembered.<ref name=Dutka1990>{{cite journal | last=Dutka | first=Jacques | title=Robert Adrain and the method of least squares | journal=Archive for History of Exact Sciences | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=41 | issue=2 | year=1990 | issn=0003-9519 | doi=10.1007/bf00411864 | pages=171–184| s2cid=123167968 }}</ref><ref name="Marquis 1607-1896">{{cite book | title = Who Was Who in America, Historical Volume, 1607–1896 | publisher = Marquis Who's Who | year = 1967}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Cite journal|last=Hogan|first=Edward R|date=1977-05-01|title=Robert Adrian: American mathematician|journal=Historia Mathematica|language=en|volume=4|issue=2|pages=157–172|doi=10.1016/0315-0860(77)90109-4|issn=0315-0860|doi-access=free}}</ref> His fields of applied mathematical interest included [[physics]], [[astronomy]] and [[geodesy]]. Many of his mathematical investigations focused on the [[shape of the Earth]].<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Swetz|first=Frank J.|date=2008|title=The Mystery of Robert Adrain|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27643138|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=81|issue=5|pages=(332–344) 333–336|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2008.11953574 |jstor=27643138 |s2cid=126151584 |issn=0025-570X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Biography==
Adrain was born in [[Carrickfergus]], [[County Antrim]], Ireland. His father, of French [[Huguenot]] descent, was a school teacher and maker of mathematical instruments, and he apparently received a good education until he was fifteen when both his parents died. He then supported himself and his four siblings by assuming his father's position as a teacher and as a private tutor.<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":2" /> In the cause of democratic reform and national independence, on 7 June 1798 he led a contingent of [[Society of United Irishmen|United Irishmen]] in the rebel army commanded by [[Henry Joy McCracken]] at the [[Battle of Antrim]].<ref>McConnell, Charles (1998), "The Aftermath of the Rising of 1798", in Archie Reid ed. ''The Liberty Tree:The story of the United Irishmen in and around the Borough of Newtownabbey'', Newtownabbery Borough Council Bi-Centenary Publication, ISBN 0953337308, (65–68), 65</ref> In the confrontation with [[British Crown]] forces, he was near fatally wounded by one of his own men. After being nursed back to health, with a bounty on his head he, his wife and infant child escaped to America.<ref name=":0" /> 

Although he was himself largely self-taught in mathematics, he secured a teaching position at the [[Princeton University|academy at Princeton]], [[New Jersey]]. In 1801 he became president of the York County Academy in [[York, Pennsylvania]]. He wrote for the ''[[Mathematical Correspondent]]'' (edited by George Baron), the first [[mathematical journal]] in the United States, contributing the first article published in America on [[Diophantine equation|diophantine algebra]]. Later he twice attempted, in 1808 and 1814, to found his own journal, ''[[The Analyst, or, Mathematical Museum]].'' While he failed to attract sufficient subscribers,<ref name=":1">{{cite book|last=Parshall|first=Karen Hunger|author-link=Karen Parshall|url=https://archive.org/details/emergenceofameri0008pars|title=The Emergence of the American Mathematical Research Community, 1876–1900|author2=David E. Rowe|author2-link=David E. Rowe|publisher=American Mathematical Society|year=1994|isbn=0-8218-9004-2|pages=[https://archive.org/details/emergenceofameri0008pars/page/43 43–44]|url-access=registration}}</ref> the first volume of the ''Analyst'' has been considered "the best collection of mathematical work produced in the United States up to that time".  As well as from Adrain, it included contributions from [[Nathaniel Bowditch]], [[Robert Patterson (educator)|Robert Patterson]], [[John Gummere]] and [[Ferdinand Rudolph Hassler]].<ref name=":0" /> Recognition followed. 

In 1809 Adrain was called to a professorship at [[Rutgers University|Rutgers (then Queen's) College]] which, in 1810, awarded him an honorary M.A.. In 1812 he was elected a Fellow of the American Philosophical Society<ref>{{Cite web|title=APS Member History|url=https://search.amphilsoc.org/memhist/search?creator=Robert+Adrain&title=&subject=&subdiv=&mem=&year=&year-max=&dead=&keyword=&smode=advanced|access-date=2021-04-02|website=search.amphilsoc.org}}</ref> and the next year, when he took a position at [[Columbia University|Columbia]], of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].<ref name="AAAS">{{cite web|title=Book of Members, 1780–2010: Chapter A|url=http://www.amacad.org/publications/BookofMembers/ChapterA.pdf|publisher=American Academy of Arts and Sciences|accessdate=6 April 2011}}</ref> From 1827 he was Professor of Mathematics in the [[University of Pennsylvania]]

In 1825, he founded a somewhat more successful publication targeting a wider readership, ''[[The Mathematical Diary]]'', which was published through 1832.<ref name=":1" /> It was fashioned after the ''Correspondent'', but at a higher level of mathematical involvement in problems solving and exposition.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Swetz|first=Frank J.|date=2008|title=The Mystery of Robert Adrain|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27643138|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=81|issue=5|pages=(332–344) 333–336|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2008.11953574 |jstor=27643138 |s2cid=126151584 |issn=0025-570X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

In 1834, Adrain was asked to resign from the University of Pennsylvania on grounds of class ill-discipline (instances of students overturning benches and throwing eggs). He returned to [[New Brunswick, New Jersey|New Brunswick]]. He rented a school room and offered private tutoring until 1836. Local records in New Brunswick indicate that during the 1830s, he held in slavery a woman named Caroline and her son Alfred.<ref>{{Cite web |title=New Jersey Slavery Records · Robert Adrain (1775-1843) |url=https://records.njslavery.org/s/doc/item/2398 |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=records.njslavery.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=New Jersey Slavery Records · 1832, Alfred, Birth |url=https://records.njslavery.org/s/doc/item/3026 |access-date=2023-11-11 |website=records.njslavery.org}}</ref>  After 1836, he returned to New York and taught at the Columbia College Grammar School before retiring to New Brunswick in 1840 where three years later he died.<ref name=":0" />

It is suggested that Adrain, today, consistent with his conviction that "the last and highest department of mathematical science consists in its application to the laws and phenomenon of the natural world", would be considered an applied mathematician. Among his broad interests in physics, astronomy and geography, his paramount concern was dynamic geodesy, specifically the mathematical investigation of the shape of the earth.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Swetz|first=Frank J.|date=2008|title=The Mystery of Robert Adrain|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/27643138|journal=Mathematics Magazine|volume=81|issue=5|pages=(332–344) 333–336|doi=10.1080/0025570X.2008.11953574 |jstor=27643138 |s2cid=126151584 |issn=0025-570X|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

Adrain was the father of Congressman [[Garnett B. Adrain]].<ref name="appletons">{{Cite Appletons'|wstitle=Adrain, Robert|year=1900}}</ref> He is commemorated by a blue plaque, unveiled at Carrickfergus by the Ulster History Circle.
